title: Myositis Autoantibodies: Jo-1, HMGCR, TIF1γ, NT5c1A and Ro52
summary: Match the main myositis-specific antibodies to their clinical subgroups (antisynthetase syndrome, necrotizing myopathy, cancer-associated and amyopathic dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis), place anti-Ro52 as an associated antibody that marks lung disease, and know why immunoprecipitation is the gold standard but hard to interpret.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 53 Hits 6, 7, 8, 9 and 15 and Exam Trap 6. Checked against Palterer 2018 (myositis autoantibody review), Mohassel 2018 (anti-HMGCR myopathy), Amlani 2019 (anti-NT5c1A), Yamaguchi 2024 (Ro52/Ro60 in anti-Jo-1 patients) and Tansley 2020 (immunoassay pitfalls). Qualified: Hit 7 “statin-associated” (statin exposure is not required; register flag rv-hmgcr-statin-naive); Hit 15 “more severe myositis and joint impairment” (muscle effect not established in the sources read; rv-ro52-ars-muscle); Hit 9 specificity is assay- and comparator-dependent (rv-nt5c1a-specificity). Not taught: the reviewer’s prevalence figures (anti-Jo-1 23–36% of PM, anti-TIF1γ 21% of myositis and 75% of cancer-associated DM, anti-MDA5 20–30%), “nonerosive” arthritis, and the epitope-spreading explanation in Trap 6.

objectives: Distinguish myositis-specific from myositis-associated autoantibodies and explain why HEp-2 ANA alone is not a myositis screen.
Match anti-Jo-1, anti-HMGCR, anti-TIF1γ, anti-MDA5 and anti-NT5c1A to their clinical subgroups.
Interpret anti-Ro52 with anti-synthetase antibodies and state the strengths and limits of immunoprecipitation and commercial immunoassays.

scenes.title: Four weak patients, four antibodies
scenes.altText: Invented scenario. Four adults with muscle weakness and a myositis antibody panel: (1) mechanic’s hands, arthritis and interstitial lung disease — anti-Jo-1; (2) on a statin, CK about 8,000 U/L, weakness persisting months after the statin was stopped — anti-HMGCR; (3) age 64, new dermatomyositis rash — anti-TIF1γ; (4) age 70, slowly worsening weakness that did not improve with steroids — anti-NT5c1A. Question token: “What does each antibody point to?”

cues.text: Four adults with muscle weakness, each with a myositis antibody panel. These cases are invented.

One has mechanic’s hands, arthritis and lung disease. One is on a statin with a very high CK. One is sixty-four with a new dermatomyositis rash. One is seventy with slow weakness that steroids did not help.
Anti-Jo-1, anti-HMGCR, anti-TIF1 gamma and anti-NT5c1A. What does each antibody point to?

props.label: What does each antibody point to?

scenes.title: Specific vs associated antibodies
scenes.altText: Concept cards (Palterer 2018; Tansley 2020). Myositis-specific autoantibodies (MSAs) are found essentially only in idiopathic inflammatory myopathy (IIM); they are generally mutually exclusive and are now detectable in over 60% of people with myositis. Myositis-associated autoantibodies (MAAs), such as anti-Ro52, anti-PM-Scl, anti-U1-RNP and anti-Ku, also occur in other connective tissue diseases. HEp-2 indirect immunofluorescence: anti-synthetase antibodies usually give a cytoplasmic pattern with a negative nucleoplasm; anti-MDA5 and anti-HMGCR are often negative or barely visible. ANA IIF should not be the sole screen for myositis antibodies.

cues.text: Myositis antibodies come in two groups. Myositis-specific antibodies are found essentially only in inflammatory myopathy, and a patient usually has just one of them.
Today one can be found in more than sixty percent of people with myositis. Each marks a fairly uniform clinical subgroup.
Myositis-associated antibodies, such as Ro52, PM-Scl, U1-RNP and Ku, also turn up in other connective tissue diseases.
On HEp-2 cells, anti-synthetase antibodies usually stain the cytoplasm, not the nucleus, and anti-MDA5 or anti-HMGCR may be nearly invisible. So an ANA alone is not a myositis screen.

props.title: Myositis-specific (MSA)
lines: Only in myositis · usually one per patient

props.title: HEp-2 IIF clues — and gaps
lines: ANA alone is not a myositis screen

scenes.title: Antibody to phenotype
scenes.altText: Four cards. Anti-Jo-1 (histidyl-tRNA synthetase): antisynthetase syndrome — myositis, arthritis, interstitial lung disease, Raynaud phenomenon, mechanic’s hands, fever; 15–25% of polymyositis/dermatomyositis; the only MSA in the 2017 EULAR/ACR classification criteria (Palterer 2018). Anti-HMGCR: immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, CK usually about 1,000–20,000 IU/L; statin exposure common but not required (statin-unexposed patients are generally younger); weakness persists after the statin is stopped and most patients need immunosuppression; not found in self-limited statin myopathy (Mohassel 2018). Anti-TIF1γ: cancer-associated adult dermatomyositis (meta-analysis: sensitivity 78%, specificity 89%, NPV 95% for cancer-associated myositis), also juvenile DM; anti-MDA5: hypo- or amyopathic DM with rapidly progressive ILD, most frequent in patients of Asian ancestry (Palterer 2018). Anti-NT5c1A (cN-1A): sporadic inclusion body myositis, sensitivity 33–80% across studies, high specificity, 6- to 9-fold higher likelihood of sIBM than polymyositis (Amlani 2019).

cues.text: Anti-Jo-1, against histidyl-transfer-RNA synthetase, defines the antisynthetase syndrome: myositis, arthritis, lung disease, Raynaud, mechanic’s hands and fever. It is the only myositis antibody in the 2017 classification criteria.

Anti-HMGCR marks immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, with CK often in the thousands. Many patients took statins, but not all. Weakness persists after the statin stops, and most need immunosuppression.

Anti-TIF1 gamma in adult dermatomyositis is a cancer flag. Its strength is a high negative predictive value. Anti-MDA5 marks dermatomyositis with little muscle disease but rapidly progressive lung disease, more common in patients of Asian ancestry.
Anti-NT5c1A points to sporadic inclusion body myositis. Sensitivity varies widely between studies, but specificity is high, which helps when the biopsy is not conclusive.

scenes.title: Ro52 and the method problem
scenes.altText: Decision cards. Anti-Ro52/TRIM21 is a myositis-associated antibody that frequently accompanies anti-synthetase antibodies (36% of 177 anti-Jo-1-positive patients in Yamaguchi 2024; Palterer 2018 cites high-titer anti-Ro52 in two-thirds of anti-Jo-1 cases, so frequency varies by cohort and assay); with anti-Jo-1 it is linked to more frequent and more severe ILD, Raynaud phenomenon and sicca symptoms; Palterer 2018 notes its effect on muscle severity has not been established. Method card: immunoprecipitation (IP) is the gold standard for most MSAs because it tests native RNA–protein complexes, but it is costly, radioactive and hard to read because non-target proteins co-precipitate and give multiple bands, so reference sera or other methods are needed (Palterer 2018). Commercial ELISA and line blots are widely used but give false positives and false negatives; blots can miss anti-TIF1γ against a conformational epitope; discordance with IIF (no cytoplasmic stain with a positive anti-synthetase result) should be flagged (Tansley 2020).

cues.text: Anti-Ro52 often rides along with anti-synthetase antibodies. In one cohort of anti-Jo-1 patients, about a third also had anti-Ro52.
With anti-Jo-1, anti-Ro52 is linked to more, and more severe, lung disease. Its effect on muscle severity is less clear.

Immunoprecipitation is the gold standard, because it tests the antigen in its native form. But it is costly, uses radioactivity, and co-precipitated proteins give extra bands that need expert reading.
Line blots and ELISAs are easier but can give false positives and negatives. Blots can miss anti-TIF1 gamma. A positive anti-synthetase with no cytoplasmic staining deserves a second look.

props.title: Anti-Ro52 + anti-synthetase
lines: More and worse ILD · muscle effect unclear

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Anti-HMGCR myopathy requires statin exposure” (✓ statin exposure is common but not required; statin-unexposed patients are usually younger); “Anti-Ro52 is a myositis-specific antibody” (✓ it is myositis-associated, also found in SLE and Sjögren syndrome; its main myositis meaning is lung disease with anti-synthetase antibodies); “Immunoprecipitation is simple to interpret” (✓ it is the gold standard, but co-precipitated proteins give multiple bands that need reference sera or other methods).

cues.text: Trap one: anti-HMGCR myopathy needs a statin. No: many patients, especially younger ones, never took one.
Trap two: anti-Ro52 is myositis-specific. No: it is myositis-associated and also occurs in lupus and Sjögren syndrome.
Trap three: immunoprecipitation is easy to read. No: it is the gold standard, but extra co-precipitated bands need expert confirmation.

cues.text: Memory aid: Jo-1 joins joints and lungs to the muscle. HMGCR hits muscle hard, statin optional. TIF1 gamma: tumor is found. NT5c1A: not treatment-responsive, inclusion body myositis.

Where it breaks: many anti-TIF1 gamma patients have no cancer, and younger ones usually have classic dermatomyositis. Anti-NT5c1A is missing in many inclusion body myositis patients and appears in some other diseases. And statins are not required for anti-HMGCR.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Jo-1 antisynthetase syndrome · HMGCR necrotizing myopathy, statin optional · TIF1γ cancer search · MDA5 rapidly progressive ILD · NT5c1A inclusion body myositis”, “Ro52 is associated, not specific · immunoprecipitation is the gold standard but needs expert reading”.

cues.text: Myositis-specific antibodies sort patients into subgroups, with anti-Jo-1 marking antisynthetase syndrome, anti-HMGCR necrotizing myopathy with or without statins, anti-TIF1 gamma a cancer search, and anti-NT5c1A inclusion body myositis.

props.label: Jo-1 synthetase · HMGCR necrotizing · TIF1γ cancer · NT5c1A sIBM
Ro52 associated, not specific · IP gold standard, hard to read

explanation.what: Plain language: in inflammatory muscle disease, the immune system makes antibodies against the body’s own proteins. Different antibodies go with different patterns of illness, so finding one tells the doctor what to look for, such as lung disease or a hidden cancer. Scientific terms: idiopathic inflammatory myopathy (IIM), myositis-specific autoantibody (MSA), myositis-associated autoantibody (MAA), aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (ARS), antisynthetase syndrome, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM), HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR), TIF1γ, MDA5, cytosolic 5′-nucleotidase 1A (NT5c1A/cN-1A), sporadic inclusion body myositis (sIBM), Ro52/TRIM21, immunoprecipitation (IP).
explanation.why: Each MSA tends to mark a fairly uniform clinical subgroup, and MSAs are generally mutually exclusive, so the antibody refines diagnosis and prognosis. MAAs such as Ro52 are less specific but can signal added risk, especially lung disease with anti-synthetase antibodies.
explanation.measure: Screening: HEp-2 IIF gives clues (cytoplasmic staining for synthetases) but anti-MDA5 and anti-HMGCR are often negative, so ANA IIF should not be the sole screen. Identification: ELISA, line blot or bead assays in routine labs; immunoprecipitation as the gold standard. Anti-HMGCR: CK usually ~1,000–20,000 IU/L. Anti-TIF1γ for cancer-associated myositis: sensitivity 78%, specificity 89%, NPV 95% (meta-analysis cited by Palterer 2018). Anti-NT5c1A for sIBM: sensitivity 33–80% across studies, specificity about 92% by ALBIA in Amlani 2019.
explanation.differs: MSA vs MAA; antisynthetase syndrome vs necrotizing myopathy vs dermatomyositis subsets vs inclusion body myositis; anti-HMGCR myopathy vs self-limited statin myopathy (no anti-HMGCR); immunoprecipitation vs commercial immunoassays.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: match an antibody to a clinical picture (mechanic’s hands and ILD → anti-Jo-1; statin and very high CK → anti-HMGCR; adult DM → cancer search with anti-TIF1γ; amyopathic DM with rapid ILD → anti-MDA5; treatment-resistant older patient → anti-NT5c1A), recognise anti-Ro52 as associated rather than specific, and know the gold-standard method.

mnemonic.text: Jo-1 JOINS joints and lungs to the muscle; HMGCR Hits muscle Hard (CK in the thousands) — statin optional; TIF1γ = Tumor Is Found; NT5c1A = Not Treatment-responsive (inclusion body myositis).
mnemonic.explanation: Links four myositis-specific antibodies to their clinical subgroups.
mnemonic.limitation: Many anti-TIF1γ patients have no cancer (positive predictive value 58% in one meta-analysis) and patients under 40 usually have classic dermatomyositis; anti-NT5c1A is absent in many sIBM patients and can occur in other diseases; statin exposure is not required for anti-HMGCR myopathy.

analogyLimitations: Antibody–phenotype links are associations; no antibody alone makes the diagnosis.
Reported frequencies vary by cohort, ancestry and assay.
takeaway: Myositis-specific antibodies sort patients into subgroups, with anti-Jo-1 marking antisynthetase syndrome, anti-HMGCR necrotizing myopathy with or without statins, anti-TIF1 gamma a cancer search, and anti-NT5c1A inclusion body myositis.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old on atorvastatin develops progressive proximal weakness with CK 9,500 U/L. Three months after the statin is stopped, weakness persists and biopsy shows a necrotizing myopathy. Which antibody is most likely?

options.rationale: Correct. Anti-HMGCR marks immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy that persists after statin withdrawal and usually needs immunosuppression.
Incorrect. Anti-Mi-2 is linked to classic dermatomyositis with skin disease and a good prognosis.
Incorrect. Anti-NT5c1A is associated with inclusion body myositis, not statin-linked necrotizing myopathy.
Incorrect. Anti-dsDNA is a marker of systemic lupus erythematosus, not a myositis antibody.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old with new dermatomyositis is positive for anti-TIF1γ. What is the most important implication?

options.text: Screen thoroughly for an underlying malignancy
options.rationale: Correct. In adults, anti-TIF1γ is associated with cancer-associated myositis (pooled sensitivity 78%, specificity 89%), so a positive result calls for a cancer search; the test is strongest at ruling out (NPV 95%).

options.text: Expect rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease
options.rationale: Incorrect. That picture fits anti-MDA5; anti-TIF1γ patients have less ILD.

options.text: Stop any statin, because the antibody is statin-induced
options.rationale: Incorrect. The statin link belongs to anti-HMGCR.
Incorrect. Inclusion body myositis is associated with anti-NT5c1A.

questions.stem: Which statement about immunoprecipitation (IP) for myositis antibodies is correct?

options.text: It is the gold standard because it tests native antigen, but co-precipitated proteins give multiple bands that need reference sera or other methods
options.rationale: Correct. IP has the best sensitivity and specificity, but it is costly, radioactive and complex to interpret.

options.text: It is the simplest, cheapest routine method
options.rationale: Incorrect. ELISA and line blots are the routine methods; IP is specialised and costly.
Incorrect. Detecting only linear epitopes is a limitation of immunoblots, which use denatured proteins.

options.text: It has been replaced because line blots never give false results
options.rationale: Incorrect. Line blots and ELISAs give false positives and false negatives, and blots can miss anti-TIF1γ.

references.usedFor: Anti-HMGCR myopathy: subacute proximal weakness, CK usually ~1,000–20,000 IU/L; most patients statin-exposed but a sizable minority (or majority in some cohorts) unexposed and generally younger; symptoms persist after statin discontinuation and most patients need immunosuppression; antibody not found in statin intolerance or self-limited statin myopathy; highly specific.

references.usedFor: Anti-NT5c1A sensitivity 0.49 and specificity 0.92 for sIBM by ALBIA; previously reported sensitivity 0.33–0.80; Larman et al. 6- to 9-fold higher likelihood of sIBM vs polymyositis; no consistent HEp-2 pattern; sIBM poorly responsive to conventional immunosuppression.

references.usedFor: Anti-Ro52 in 36% and anti-Ro60 in 15% of 177 anti-Jo-1-positive patients; anti-Ro52 with anti-Jo-1 linked to increased prevalence/severity of ILD, Raynaud phenomenon and sicca symptoms; prior studies link the combination with mechanic’s hands and malignancy; anti-Ro52 also found in SLE and Sjögren syndrome; anti-Jo-1 15–30% of myositis.

references.citation: Tansley SL, Snowball J, Pauling JD, et al. The promise, perceptions, and pitfalls of immunoassays for autoantibody testing in myositis. Arthritis Res Ther. 2020;22(1):117. doi:10.1186/s13075-020-02210-2
references.usedFor: MSAs detectable in over 60% of myositis and generally mutually exclusive; commercial immunoassays (ELISA, line blot) widely used with concerns about false positives and negatives; blotting assays can miss anti-TIF1γ against a conformational epitope; discordance with IIF (no cytoplasmic staining with positive anti-synthetase) often not highlighted; IP preferred as gold standard where available.

claims.text: MSA vs MAA definitions, mutual exclusivity, >60% detection, HEp-2 IIF clues and gaps.
Anti-Jo-1 and antisynthetase syndrome features; only MSA in the 2017 criteria.
Anti-HMGCR necrotizing myopathy: CK range, statin common but not required, persists after withdrawal, absent in self-limited statin myopathy.
Anti-TIF1γ cancer association and test performance; anti-MDA5 amyopathic DM with RP-ILD, most frequent in Asian ancestry.
Anti-NT5c1A for sIBM: variable sensitivity, high specificity, 6- to 9-fold likelihood; sIBM poorly responsive to immunosuppression.
Anti-Ro52 is myositis-associated, often with ARS, linked to more severe ILD; muscle effect not established.
IP gold standard but complex; immunoassay pitfalls.

Reviewer prevalence figures (anti-Jo-1 23–36% of PM; anti-TIF1γ 21% of myositis and 75% of cancer-associated adult DM; anti-MDA5 20–30%), “nonerosive” arthritis in antisynthetase syndrome, and intermolecular epitope spreading as the reason IP is hard to interpret.
claims.note: Not taught; the sources read give different or no figures, and attribute IP complexity to co-precipitation of complexed proteins.

claims.text: “Jo joins, TIF tells, NT never responds.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 53 Hit 7 labels anti-HMGCR as a marker of statin-associated necrotizing myopathy. Mohassel 2018 and Palterer 2018 report that statin exposure is not required: a sizable minority (the majority in some cohorts) of anti-HMGCR myopathy patients, generally younger, never took statins (register flag rv-hmgcr-statin-naive).

Ch. 53 Hit 15 says anti-Ro52 with anti-ARS means more severe myositis and joint impairment. Palterer 2018 states the role of anti-Ro52 in muscle severity has not been identified (its prognostic weight is for ILD); Yamaguchi 2024 found more and worse ILD, Raynaud and sicca, citing one earlier study for myositis activity and earlier studies for mechanic’s hands and malignancy; neither source supports more joint impairment (register flag rv-ro52-ars-muscle).

Ch. 53 Hit 9 gives anti-NT5c1A >90% specificity. Specificity depends on assay and comparator group: Amlani 2019 found 91.8% by ALBIA (with no positives in its rheumatoid arthritis, primary Sjögren or juvenile dermatomyositis groups), but Palterer 2018 cites other reports of anti-cN-1A in about 30% of Sjögren syndrome and 20% of SLE, and in 12% of healthy children (register flag rv-nt5c1a-specificity).

verification.notes: 7 claims checked against Palterer 2018, Mohassel 2018, Amlani 2019, Yamaguchi 2024 and Tansley 2020 (all full text via Europe PMC); 1 pending (reviewer prevalence figures, “nonerosive” arthritis, epitope-spreading explanation). No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
